```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This analysis is adapted from DATASCI 306 HW5. It demonstrates reading a local CSV, auditing missing values, writing reusable R functions, avoiding repeated-measure counting, visualizing patterns, and applying a chi-squared test. The source dataset is the `storms` CSV from `dplyr` v1.1.4 (1975-2022).

## 1. Read and validate the CSV

The input CSV is stored at `data/storms.csv`. Open the `.Rproj` file to set the working directory to the repository root.

```{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

storms <- read_csv("data/storms.csv", na = c("", "NA"), show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(storms) == 19537L)
head(storms)
```

## 2. Audit missing values

```{r missing}
missing_counts <- storms |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)
print(missing_counts)
```

Missing `category` means the system was not a hurricane. Since wind and pressure have no missing values in this CSV, the key variables for the later analysis do not require imputation.

## 3. Custom function: count distinct hurricanes

Each named storm may appear in multiple six-hour observations. Counting rows would therefore exaggerate hurricane frequency. The following function counts each hurricane only once per year and separately tracks storms that ever reached Category 5.

```{r custom-function-1}
annual_hurricane_counts <- function(df) {
  df |>
    group_by(year, name) |>
    summarise(
      is_hurricane = any(status == "hurricane"),
      is_cat5 = any(category == 5, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(hurricanes = sum(is_hurricane),
              category5 = sum(is_cat5), .groups = "drop")
}

yearly <- annual_hurricane_counts(storms)
head(yearly)
```

```{r annual-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
p1 <- yearly |>
  pivot_longer(c(hurricanes, category5),
               names_to = "type", values_to = "n") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1B6A84", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Annual hurricane activity (1975-2022)",
       x = "Year", y = "Number of distinct storms") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
p1
```

## 4. Use one representative observation per storm

To reduce repeated-observation bias in inference, keep the highest-wind record for each distinct `(year, name)` storm.

```{r peak-observation}
peak <- storms |>
  filter(!is.na(wind), !is.na(pressure)) |>
  group_by(year, name) |>
  slice_max(order_by = wind, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()
stopifnot(nrow(peak) == 655L)
```

## 5. Custom function: categorize continuous variables

The function creates three quantile-based bins, while checking that the quantile breakpoints are distinct.

```{r custom-function-2}
to_tercile <- function(x) {
  cuts <- quantile(x, probs = c(1/3, 2/3), na.rm = TRUE)
  if (cuts[1] >= cuts[2]) stop("Tercile breakpoints must differ")
  cut(x, breaks = c(-Inf, cuts, Inf),
      labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
      include.lowest = TRUE)
}
```

## 6. Chi-squared association test

We test whether peak wind-speed categories and central-pressure categories are independent. Both variables are discretized to satisfy the input requirements of the chi-squared test.

```{r statistical-test}
peak <- peak |>
  mutate(wind_group = to_tercile(wind),
         pressure_group = to_tercile(pressure))
frequency <- with(peak, table(wind_group, pressure_group))
chi <- chisq.test(frequency)
print(frequency)
print(chi)
cat("Minimum expected count:", min(chi$expected), "\n")
cat("Pearson correlation:", cor(peak$wind, peak$pressure), "\n")
```

The test finds a statistically significant association: stronger peak winds tend to accompany lower central pressures. This is an association, not a causal inference, and the categories were constructed from continuous measurements.

## 7. Visualize the relationship and save figures

```{r pressure-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
p2 <- ggplot(peak, aes(x = wind, y = pressure)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1B6A84", alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#D4764E") +
  labs(title = "Wind speed and pressure at storm peak",
       x = "Peak wind speed (knots)",
       y = "Central pressure (mb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
p2
```

```{r save-plots}
ggsave("figures/annual_hurricane_counts.png", plot = p1,
       width = 7, height = 4.2, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/storm_peak_wind_pressure.png", plot = p2,
       width = 7, height = 4.2, dpi = 300)
```
